title: Megaspeed exec was recruited to spy on Nvidia CEO, according to US intelligence memo
content:
A memo circulated earlier this year claimed that technology executive Alice Huang was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to multiple media reports.
The New York Times, which had previously said Nvidia’s chief executive had been the target of Chinese intelligence, was the first to report on the memo, which was reportedly based on U.S. intelligence. The Financial Times subsequently reported that the memo also claimed Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed.
An Nvidia spokesperson told the NYT that Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual,” and that the company does not share classified information with its customers.
A separate NYT report examined New Matrix, a Chinese company authorized by the U.S. Commerce Department to buy advanced Nvidia chips. But at the office address listed by New Matrix, reporters only found “a hollow gray shell,” raising concerns that it could be a front for a blacklisted private equity firm.
The Nvidia spokesperson said the company sells “the first, best and most of our technology in America.”

report.summary: A US intelligence memo reportedly claims a Megaspeed executive was recruited by China to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, raising chip-export and corporate-security concerns.
report.background: The report lands at the intersection of AI-chip geopolitics and corporate espionage. Nvidia’s advanced GPUs are central to the AI boom and are tightly controlled under US export rules, making the company and its CEO high-value intelligence targets. According to media reports, a memo based on US intelligence claims Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Jensen Huang; the Financial Times reportedly added a claim of a romantic relationship. Nvidia says Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual” and that it does not share classified information with customers. A separate New York Times report examined New Matrix, a Commerce Department-authorized Nvidia chip buyer, and found only an empty office, raising concerns about front companies and export-control loopholes.
key_points: A memo reportedly based on US intelligence claims Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The New York Times first reported the memo; the Financial Times later reported an additional claim of a romantic relationship. The allegations are unconfirmed and the memo is not public.

Nvidia pushed back on the memo’s implications. A spokesperson said Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual” and that Nvidia does not share classified information with customers. The company also stressed that it sells “the first, best and most of our technology in America,” signaling concern about export-control and trust issues.

A separate NYT report examined New Matrix, a Chinese company authorized by the US Commerce Department to buy advanced Nvidia chips. Reporters found only “a hollow gray shell” at its listed office address, raising concerns that it could be a front for a blacklisted private equity firm.

The episode highlights how AI chips, cloud providers and authorized buyers have become intelligence and compliance battlegrounds. Third-party GPU clouds and resellers can obscure who ultimately uses advanced Nvidia hardware, making due diligence on executives, ownership and customers more urgent for US regulators and chipmakers.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the report is likely to intensify scrutiny of GPU cloud providers, resellers and export-control intermediaries. Companies that handle advanced Nvidia chips may face tougher Know-Your-Customer checks, ownership reviews and reputational risk, even without proven wrongdoing. Developers who rely on third-party clouds for scarce GPU capacity could see more delays, documentation requests or access restrictions as providers tighten compliance. Regular users are less directly affected, but the case reinforces how geopolitical trust and supply-chain security shape AI service availability, pricing and privacy. Nvidia’s response also shows how reputational and national-security claims can quickly become corporate-governance issues. The key takeaway is that AI infrastructure is now a security asset, not just a commercial product.
